title: Incrementality, pull-forward and the post-promotion dip
reading_md:
**What it is.** Incremental sales are the sales that would not have happened without the promotion. The gross lift over the baseline mixes three things:

- switching from your other products (cannibalisation);
- purchases pulled forward from later weeks (stockpiling), seen as a post-promotion dip;
- true extra demand (category expansion).

The baseline and the uplift itself are in the reading **Promo uplift vs baseline**, and cannibalisation and halo have their own readings.

A study of every promotion a large US drugstore chain ran in 2003 (Ailawadi and colleagues, Marketing Science, 2007) found that about 45% of the gross lift was incremental. Each unit of gross lift came with 0.16 units of other products bought elsewhere in the store, a halo. More than half of the promotions were not profitable. From a field test, the authors projected that ending promotions in the 15 worst categories would cut sales by about $7.8M but raise profit by about $52.6M. Post-promotion dips are stronger for high-priced, frequently promoted, high-share items.

**How to work it out.**

Incremental units = gross lift - cannibalised units - pulled-forward units (+ halo units when you measure the whole store)

Worked example. A promotion week sells 1,500 units against a baseline of 1,000. Sister products lose 150 units, and the next two weeks are 100 units below baseline in total.

- Gross lift = 1,500 - 1,000 = 500.
- Incremental = 500 - 150 - 100 = 250 units.
- 250 / 500 = 50% of the gross lift (whole units, whole percent).

**In the interview.** "A promotion doubled sales. Did it work?" A model answer: "I cannot tell yet. I would measure against a baseline, net out cannibalisation and the post-promotion dip, then check contribution after the discount."

**Common mistakes.**

- Calling the whole bump incremental.
- Looking only at the promotion weeks, so the dip is missed.
- Assuming every category behaves alike. A study of store data (Leeflang and colleagues, 2008) found small stockpiling effects (6%), modest cross-item effects (22%) and large category-expansion effects (72%).
